options.A: A blueprint that translates strategy into action by specifying tactics, target market, customer needs, and how the firm makes money.
options.B: A mission statement that describes values and purpose, while leaving tactics, target market, and revenue logic to emerge later, overall.
options.C: A governance charter that specifies director duties and audit requirements, while leaving customer value and pricing to markets, in practice.
options.D: A five-forces map that identifies entry, rivalry, substitutes, and bargaining power, while leaving revenue capture unspecified in practice, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The textbook defines business models as translating strategy into action: tactics and initiatives, target market and customer needs, and the revenue logic for making money. Mission, governance charters, and five forces are related but not the business model definition. Distractor Misconceptions: B: Confuses business model with purpose/mission statements. C: Confuses business model with governance and compliance design. D: Confuses industry structure analysis with revenue and value capture logic.
2yr-20.stem: In the chapter, a business model is defined most precisely as:

options.A: Why: value proposition and rationale; Who: target customers and stakeholders; What: offerings; How: revenue and delivery logic, in practice.
options.B: Why: product features; Who: regulators only; What: board committees; How: hostile takeover defenses such as poison pills in practice.
options.C: Why: cost structure; Who: suppliers only; What: audit standards; How: analysts’ buy-hold-sell recommendations over time, overall, as stated here.
options.D: Why: legal compliance; Who: courts; What: penalties; How: prosecutions that substitute for business model design in practice, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The framework guides leaders to define rationale/value, offerings, customers, and execution/revenue logic. The other options misplace governance and compliance items into the business model framework. Distractor Misconceptions: B: Confuses business model elements with governance/takeover mechanics. C: Confuses customers and offerings with suppliers and audits. D: Reduces business models to legal penalties and prosecution.
2yr-20.stem: In the business model framework (why–what–who–how), which pairing is most accurate?

options.A: Razor-and-blade (bait-and-hook), where a durable platform is sold near cost while high-margin consumables generate profits, overall, as stated here.
options.B: Freemium, where a free version attracts users and a premium tier monetizes power users through feature gating over time.
options.C: Wholesale, where retailers buy at a discount and set resale prices, earning margin mainly through inventory turnover in practice.
options.D: Pay-as-you-go, where usage is metered and customers pay only for consumption without lock-in or proprietary complements, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page explicitly frames Nespresso as bait-and-hook: machines (bait) and proprietary pods (hook), reinforced by lock-in. That differs from freemium, wholesale, or usage-metered pay-as-you-go models. Distractor Misconceptions: B: Confuses consumable lock-in with feature-gated software freemium. C: Confuses proprietary ecosystem lock-in with retail channel wholesaling. D: Confuses lock-in consumables with non-lock-in metered pricing.
2yr-20.stem: Nespresso is presented as an example of which business model logic on the course page?

options.A: Better demand forecasting that reduces spoilage and middlemen costs, improving unit economics in a perishable supply chain, overall.
options.B: Lower threat of entry, because subscriptions legally prevent competitors from offering similar products in the same market, overall.
options.C: Lower buyer power, because subscription customers cannot cancel without regulatory approval and therefore become captive in practice, overall.
options.D: Higher supplier power, because subscriptions force farms to accept lower prices and therefore raise margins automatically over time.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page highlights subscription enabling forecasting and reduced spoilage, especially in perishables. Subscriptions do not legally block entry, nor do they make cancellation impossible; supplier power effects are not automatic. Distractor Misconceptions: B: Assumes contracts legally prevent competitive entry. C: Assumes subscriptions make customers legally captive. D: Assumes subscription automatically weakens suppliers regardless of structure.
2yr-20.stem: Country Delight is used on the course page to illustrate which primary business model advantage of subscription?

options.A: Asset ownership and working-capital discipline that enable low costs and low prices, reinforced by limited SKUs and cash discounts, overall.
options.B: Freemium sampling and viral loops that enable low customer acquisition costs, reinforced by network effects and referral incentives, in practice.
options.C: Poison pills and takeover defenses that enable low costs by stabilizing control, reinforced by premium pricing and exclusivity in practice.
options.D: Long-tail assortment and infinite shelf space that enable low prices, reinforced by niche variety and algorithmic discovery over time, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page notes ownership choices, limited SKUs, and fast supplier payments to secure discounts—classic EDLC/EDLP mechanics. The other options are software platform or takeover tools or long-tail logic, not D‑Mart’s described model. Distractor Misconceptions: B: Confuses retail cost discipline with software acquisition loops and network effects. C: Confuses takeover defense with cost leadership drivers. D: Confuses EDLP with long-tail variety and infinite shelf space.
2yr-20.stem: D‑Mart’s EDLC–EDLP model is described on the course page as relying most directly on:

options.A: Products are negatively correlated in demand, so the bundle’s perceived value can exceed the sum of parts for many customers.
options.B: Products are perfect substitutes, so bundling reduces competition by eliminating choice and forcing single-product adoption in practice, as stated here.
options.C: Products are commodities, so bundling creates lock-in solely by raising the list price without changing willingness to pay over time.
options.D: Products are perishable, so bundling ensures forecasting accuracy and therefore eliminates spoilage without subscription commitments, overall, as described, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page emphasizes bundling negatively correlated products to create a ‘walled garden’ where value exceeds parts. Substitutes, list-price inflation, or perishability are not the core mechanism described. Distractor Misconceptions: B: Confuses complements/bundles with substitutes and forced adoption. C: Assumes bundling works by price inflation rather than value perception. D: Confuses bundling with subscription-based forecasting and spoilage reduction.
2yr-20.stem: Bundling is described on the course page as especially powerful when:

options.A: Selling small volumes of many niche items becomes feasible when technology lowers distribution and search costs, expanding selection, as stated here.
options.B: Selling large volumes of a few blockbuster items is feasible when technology lowers distribution costs, shrinking selection in practice, in practice.
options.C: Selling niche items requires physical shelf space expansion, so long-tail success depends mainly on owning more retail real estate over time.
options.D: Selling niche items depends mainly on takeover defenses, because acquisition threats force firms to focus on blockbusters in practice, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: Long tail is ‘selling less of more’: digitization and search lower distribution frictions and enable niche demand to be served. It is not primarily about blockbusters, physical shelf space, or takeover defenses. Distractor Misconceptions: B: Reverses the short-head vs long-tail logic. C: Assumes physical shelf-space expansion is the key enabler. D: Misattributes product assortment choices to takeover defenses.
2yr-20.stem: The long tail concept is best summarized (as in the course page and textbook) as:

options.A: Crowdsourcing and wisdom of crowds across the value chain, reducing downside by producing only designs validated by the community, overall.
options.B: Poison-pill governance that prevents hostile takeovers, reducing downside by avoiding acquisition premiums and winner’s curse in practice, as stated here.
options.C: Freemium pricing that converts users into paying customers by locking premium designs behind a paywall and limiting access over time.
options.D: Wholesale distribution that shifts inventory risk to retailers, reducing downside by requiring retailers to prepay for all designs in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The textbook describes Threadless as crowdsourcing design, forecasting, and demand validation (‘I’d buy it’), producing only community-approved designs to reduce downside. The other options confuse business model innovation mechanisms. Distractor Misconceptions: B: Confuses takeover defenses with crowdsourced production economics. C: Confuses crowdsourcing with freemium feature gating. D: Confuses community validation with wholesale inventory risk shifting.
2yr-20.stem: Threadless (textbook) best illustrates which business model innovation mechanism?

options.A: Strategy sets the goal-directed competitive approach; the business model specifies the tactics and revenue logic that operationalize it, in practice.
options.B: Strategy is pricing tactics; the business model is industry structure; governance then sets customer value and product positioning in practice.
options.C: Strategy is the board’s job; the business model is the regulator’s job; managers only execute without discretion in practice, overall.
options.D: Strategy is ethics; the business model is legality; governance is marketing; so each operates in separate silos over time, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter explicitly positions business models as ‘strategy in action’: translating strategic intent into concrete initiatives and revenue logic. The other options scramble the relationships. Distractor Misconceptions: B: Misassigns industry structure to business model and pricing to strategy. C: Misassigns roles to regulators and removes managerial agency. D: Artificially partitions ethics, legality, and marketing into separate silos.
2yr-20.stem: Which diagnosis best distinguishes ‘strategy’ from ‘business model’ in the chapter’s framing?

options.A: Business model innovation that changes economics and distribution, even when underlying product technology is not radically new, in practice.
options.B: Radical product technology that makes competitors obsolete, even when distribution and pricing remain unchanged in practice, as stated here.
options.C: Takeover defenses that prevent incumbents from acquiring entrants, making disruption legally protected over time, in practice, as stated here.
options.D: GAAP reporting differences that hide true costs, making disruption an accounting artifact rather than real value creation in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter highlights Dollar Shave Club as business model innovation disrupting an incumbent—changing how value is delivered and captured rather than relying on breakthrough blade technology. Distractor Misconceptions: B: Over-attributes disruption to product tech rather than economics and distribution. C: Assumes disruption depends on legal protection from acquisitions. D: Misstates disruption as an accounting illusion.
2yr-20.stem: Dollar Shave Club is used in the chapter as evidence that disruptive advantage can come mainly from:

options.A: Managers must adapt tactics, partners, and revenue logic as environments shift; a once-effective model can become obsolete over time, as stated here.
options.B: Business models never change once chosen, because stability guarantees competitive advantage and adaptation signals strategic weakness in practice, in the scenario, overall.
options.C: Business models change only when regulators rewrite accounting rules, because revenue logic is determined by GAAP rather than by design choices, overall.
options.D: Business models change only through hostile takeovers, because acquisitions are the only mechanism that can alter how firms make money in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter treats business models as evolving: changes in technology, competition, or customer behavior can require adaptation. They are not fixed, not determined solely by accounting, and not changed only via takeovers. Distractor Misconceptions: B: Assumes stability is always optimal and adaptation is weakness. C: Confuses accounting rules with business model design. D: Assumes takeovers are the only driver of model change.
2yr-20.stem: Which statement best captures why business models are ‘dynamic’ in the chapter?

options.A: Different profit drivers within similar markets, where the ‘how’ of the business model differs even when the ‘what’ looks similar, in practice.
options.B: Different governance mechanisms, where one firm uses a poison pill and the other uses GAAP audits to create competitive advantage in practice.
options.C: Different industry structures, where one operates in monopoly and the other in perfect competition, so business models do not matter over time.
options.D: Different ethics codes, where one has values and the other lacks them, so economics follow automatically from moral superiority in practice, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page contrasts aggregator vs logistics models (e.g., Zomato vs Swiggy) in profit drivers—how value is captured. That is a business model difference, not a governance or ethics label by itself. Distractor Misconceptions: B: Confuses business model profit logic with governance tools. C: Assumes market structure alone determines profits, denying business model choices. D: Assumes ethics alone determines economics automatically.
2yr-20.stem: A platform aggregator earns from ads and discovery, while a logistics-focused competitor earns from delivery fees and membership. This contrast best illustrates:

options.A: Too few buyers and sellers exist in each niche, so matching is hard unless technology aggregates demand and supply across boundaries.
options.B: Too many buyers exist in each niche, so matching is easy and technology therefore cannot add value in practice, in practice.
options.C: Too many suppliers exist, so supplier power collapses and firms must rely on takeover defenses rather than matching over time, overall.
options.D: Too few regulators exist, so markets cannot function and business models must be replaced by legal enforcement in practice, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: Thin markets arise when there are too few participants for efficient matching. Aggregation and search technology can help—central to long-tail viability. Distractor Misconceptions: B: Reverses the problem: abundance is not thinness. C: Confuses thin markets with supplier power and takeover defense logic. D: Confuses market participation with regulatory headcount.
2yr-20.stem: Which situation best illustrates ‘thin markets’ as a barrier to long-tail success?

options.A: Complexity without value creation, if added tactics increase costs and confusion without improving customer value or unit economics, in practice.
options.B: Guaranteed lock-in, because adding tactics always increases switching costs regardless of customer perception in practice, overall, as described, in practice.
options.C: Guaranteed ethics, because bundling and subscription reduce incentives to misreport and therefore eliminate bad-barrel risks over time, as stated here.
options.D: Guaranteed takeover immunity, because bundled customers prevent hostile bidders from paying premiums and therefore stop corporate control markets in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter treats business models as translating strategy into actionable economics; adding tactics can backfire if it adds complexity without improving value or margins. Lock-in, ethics, and takeover immunity are not automatic. Distractor Misconceptions: B: Assumes tactics always increase switching costs and lock-in. C: Assumes business model choices eliminate ethical risk automatically. D: Assumes customers prevent hostile bids and premiums automatically.
2yr-20.stem: A firm combines subscription with an ecosystem bundle. Which risk is most consistent with the chapter’s emphasis on ‘strategy in action’?

options.A: Freemium, because a free version acquires users while a paid version monetizes a subset through feature gating and convenience, overall.
options.B: Subscription only, because all recurring payments are subscriptions regardless of free tiers, ads, and conversion funnels in practice, in practice.
options.C: Wholesale only, because free tiers are equivalent to bulk discounts given to retailers who then set resale prices in practice.
options.D: Razor-and-blade only, because all recurring revenue must come from consumables rather than from upgrades and service bundles in practice, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: A free tier plus paid upgrade is the canonical freemium structure. Subscription can be part of the paid tier, but the defining feature is the free-to-paid conversion funnel; wholesale and razor-and-blade are different logics. Distractor Misconceptions: B: Treats subscription as a catch‑all label and ignores the free-to-paid funnel. C: Confuses end-user tiers with retail channel wholesaling. D: Restricts recurring revenue to consumables and mislabels upgrades.

options.A: Freemium, because a free version acquires users while a paid version monetizes a subset through feature gating and convenience, overall.
options.B: Subscription only, because all recurring payments are subscriptions regardless of free tiers, ads, and conversion funnels in practice, in practice.
options.C: Wholesale only, because free tiers are equivalent to bulk discounts given to retailers who then set resale prices in practice.
options.D: Razor-and-blade only, because all recurring revenue must come from consumables rather than from upgrades and service bundles in practice, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: A free tier plus paid upgrade is the canonical freemium structure. Subscription can be part of the paid tier, but the defining feature is the free-to-paid conversion funnel; wholesale and razor-and-blade are different logics. Distractor Misconceptions: B: Treats subscription as a catch‑all label and ignores the free-to-paid funnel. C: Confuses end-user tiers with retail channel wholesaling. D: Restricts recurring revenue to consumables and mislabels upgrades.

options.A: Freemium, because a free version acquires users while a paid version monetizes a subset through feature gating and convenience, overall.
options.B: Subscription only, because all recurring payments are subscriptions regardless of free tiers, ads, and conversion funnels in practice, in practice.

2yr-20.stem: A firm offers a free tier with ads and a paid tier with premium features (Item 25). Which label fits best?

options.A: Both are examples of excellent Guiding Policies, but different in implementation.
options.B: Twitter is displaying "Strategic Ambition," while Tesla is displaying "Operational Effectiveness."
options.C: Twitter is mistaking a "Goal" for a "Strategy," while Tesla is demonstrating a "Guiding Policy" and "Coherent Actions."
options.D: Tesla is falling into the "Red Queen Effect" by telegraphing its moves, while Twitter is maintaining strategic flexibility.

2yr-03.stem: 1: The Definition of Strategy (Case: Twitter vs. Tesla) Case Let: In 2020, Twitter (now X) executives stated their primary objective was "to have the largest daily active user base in the world." Conversely, in 2006, Elon Musk published a blog post for Tesla detailing a sequence: "Build sports car -> Use money to build affordable car -> Use money to build mass market car." Based on Section 1.1, how would a strategic analyst classify these two approaches?

options.A: Jio has a Sustainable Competitive Advantage because it was the first mover.
options.B: Airtel has a Competitive Disadvantage because it was forced to react to Jio.
options.C: Both firms have achieved Competitive Parity relative to each other.
options.D: Both firms are suffering from the Red Queen Effect and destroying industry value.

2yr-03.stem: 2: Competitive Advantage vs. Parity (Case: Jio vs. Airtel) Case Let: In the Indian telecom sector, Reliance Jio launched with free data, disrupting the market. By 2023, Bharti Airtel had matched Jio’s pricing structure and 5G rollout speed. Both firms now hold dominant market shares and return similar profit margins that are slightly above the industry average, while Vodafone-Idea continues to lose market share. How would you classify the relationship between Jio and Airtel as per LO 1-2?

options.A: Failure to Identify Stakeholders.
options.B: Stuck in the Middle (Failure to resolve Trade-offs).
options.C: The Red Queen Effect.
options.D: Lack of Corporate Social Responsibility.

2yr-03.stem: 3: Strategic Trade-offs (Case: Tata Nano vs. Maruti Suzuki) Case Let: Tata Motors attempted to launch the "Nano" as the world's cheapest car (Cost Leadership). However, they also marketed it as a safe, aspirational family vehicle (Differentiation). The car failed to dominate the market, as consumers perceived it as "cheap" (low status) rather than "valuable." Meanwhile, Maruti Suzuki maintained a middle-market position. Which strategic concept from Section 1.1 best explains Tata's failure with the Nano?

options.A: Yes, because it improved their profit margins.
options.B: No, this is Operational Effectiveness, which is necessary but not sufficient for advantage.
options.C: Yes, because they implemented a "Guiding Policy" of quality control.
options.D: No, because they did not consult external stakeholders.

2yr-03.stem: 4: Strategy vs. Operational Effectiveness (Case: Infosys vs. Wipro) Case Let: Two Indian IT giants, Infosys and Wipro, decide to implement the exact same "Agile" software development methodology and "Six Sigma" quality controls to reduce bugs by 10%. They both succeed in lowering costs by 5%. Does this constitute a strategy?

options.A: Economic Power (They held a large equity stake).
options.B: Legal Power (They were a government regulator).
options.C: Legitimacy and Urgency.
options.D: Corporate Social Responsibility.

2yr-03.stem: 1: The Black Swan & Stakeholders (Case: Adani Group 2023) Case Let: In early 2023, the Hindenburg Research report accused the Adani Group of financial irregularities. This event, unexpected and high-impact, caused a massive stock sell-off. The "Short Seller" (Hindenburg) had no formal power over Adani but managed to crash the stock. In the context of Stakeholder Impact Analysis (LO 1-4), which attribute did Hindenburg primarily leverage to gain "Power"?

options.A: There is no risk; Shareholder Primacy is the only law.
options.B: Loss of Legitimacy and erosion of Competitive Advantage due to broken exchange relationships.
options.C: Improvement in the "Red Queen" position.
options.D: An increase in "Consumer Surplus."

2yr-03.stem: 2: Stakeholder Trade-offs (Case: Zomato) Case Let: Zomato faces pressure from investors (Internal) to increase profitability (Unit Economics). Simultaneously, delivery partners (External) strike for higher payouts per delivery. Zomato decides to cut delivery partner pay to satisfy investor margin calls. According to Stakeholder Theory (Section 1.2), what is the long-term risk of this decision?

options.A: Economic Responsibility (The Base).
options.B: Legal Responsibility.
options.C: Ethical Responsibility.
options.D: Philanthropic Responsibility.

2yr-03.stem: 3: CSR Pyramid (Case: Starbucks) Case Let: In 2018, Starbucks closed 8,000 stores for a day to conduct racial bias training after an incident in Philadelphia. This cost them millions in lost revenue and was not mandated by any judge. Where does this action fall on Carroll’s Pyramid of CSR (Section 1.2)?

options.A: Step 1: Identifying Stakeholders.
options.B: Step 2: Identifying Interests.
options.C: Step 5: Addressing Stakeholder Concerns.
options.D: Step 4: Philanthropy.

2yr-03.stem: 4: Impact Analysis Step 5 (Case: Nestle Maggi Crisis) Case Let: When lead was allegedly found in Maggi noodles in India, Nestle initially denied the claims. Regulators (Govt) banned the product. Consumers (Society) boycotted. Nestle eventually destroyed 30,000 tonnes of product and relaunched with transparency. In the 5-Step Stakeholder Impact Analysis, where did Nestle initially fail?

options.A: Formulation (F).
options.B: Implementation (I).
options.C: Analysis (A).
options.D: Strategic Control.

2yr-03.stem: 1: Diagnosis (Case: SpaceX) Case Let: Before SpaceX, the aerospace industry believed space travel was expensive due to fuel costs. Elon Musk’s "First Principles" thinking revealed the problem wasn't fuel, but the fact that rockets were discarded after one use. Which phase of the AFI Framework does this insight represent?

options.A: A Diagnosis of the challenge.
options.B: A Guiding Policy to address the challenge.
options.C: Competitive Parity.
options.D: Philanthropic Responsibility.

2yr-03.stem: 2: Guiding Policy (Case: Netflix) Case Let: In 2011, Netflix realized streaming was the future. They decided to pivot away from DVD-by-mail, split the services (Qwikster debacle), and invest heavily in original content (House of Cards) to differentiate from cable TV. The decision to invest in original content represents:

options.A: Grandiose Statements.
options.B: Coherent Actions.
options.C: External Stakeholders.
options.D: Black Swan Events.

2yr-03.stem: 3: Implementation (Case: Apple) Case Let: Apple’s strategy emphasizes premium differentiation. To support this, they build their own chips (M1/M2), control their retail stores, and maintain a closed ecosystem (iOS). These specific activities (Stores, Chips, iOS) are best described as:

options.A: The Blue Ocean Strategy.
options.B: The Red Queen Effect.
options.C: Stakeholder Impact Analysis.
options.D: Strategic Commitments.

2yr-03.stem: 1: The Red Queen Effect (Case: Coca-Cola vs. Pepsi) Case Let: For decades, Coke and Pepsi have spent billions on advertising. If Coke spends $1B, Pepsi spends $1B. Their market shares remain relatively stable despite the massive spend. Which strategic phenomenon describes this situation?

options.A: They have a Competitive Disadvantage because their price is low.
options.B: They have a Competitive Advantage because their Economic Value Created (V-C) is higher.
options.C: They have Competitive Parity.
options.D: They are stuck in the middle.

2yr-03.stem: 2: Economic Value Creation (Case: Aldi) Case Let: Aldi (German retailer) offers goods at a much lower price (P) than competitors. However, their Cost (C) to operate is so incredibly low due to no-frills stores that the gap between Value (V) and Cost (C) is actually larger than traditional supermarkets. What does this imply about Aldi's Competitive Advantage?

options.A: Failure to define the competitive challenge (Diagnosis).
options.B: Lack of capital (Implementation).
options.C: Too much focus on Stakeholders.
options.D: Failure to execute the Red Queen effect.

2yr-03.stem: 3: Strategic Leadership (Case: Kodak) Case Let: Kodak invented the digital camera but filed for bankruptcy because its leadership refused to pivot from film, fearing it would cannibalize their existing profits. According to Section 1.4 (Implications for Leaders), what was the primary failure?

options.A: Because the first plan failed.
options.B: Because strategy is static and never changes.
options.C: Because strategy is a continuous process; once the initial diagnosis is solved, new challenges (scaling, autonomy) arise requiring new policies.
options.D: To distract shareholders from low profits.

2yr-03.stem: 4: Master Plan Part Deux (Case: Tesla 2016) Case Let: In 2016, Elon Musk updated his strategy. He announced goals to "Expand the EV product line to all major segments" and "Develop self-driving capability 10x safer than manual." Why was this necessary according to the concept of Strategic Management (LO 1-1)?

options.A: Shaping industry structure by expanding the profit pool.
options.B: Positioning the company where the competitive forces are weakest.
options.C: Exploiting industry change by creating a new substitute.
options.D: Neutralizing supplier power through vertical integration.

2yr-05.explanation: This is the exact Paccar strategy from the HBR article and your teaching script. The company is not trying to change the "terrible" structure of the entire airline industry. Instead, it is engaging in Positioning. It has identified a "foxhole" or niche segment (owner-operators in Paccar's case, executives here) where the force of Buyer Power is weak, allowing it to escape the intense, price-based rivalry of the main industry.
2yr-05.stem: A company in a "terrible" industry (e.g., airlines) decides to exclusively serve a small, fragmented customer niche (e.g., high-net-worth executives) that is far less price-sensitive and demands hyper-customized service. According to Porter, this is a classic example of:

options.A: A new entrant.
options.B: A substitute.
options.C: A rival.
options.D: A complementor.

2yr-05.explanation: This tests the "job-to-be-done" concept from your teaching script (e.g., Twitter vs. TikTok). The "job" a movie theater sells is "leisure time" or "filling 90 minutes of downtime." A mobile game performs the exact same job through a different means. It is not a rival (it's not a theater) or a new entrant (it's not entering the theater industry). It is a powerful substitute that competes for the customer's time and leisure budget.
2yr-05.stem: A free-to-play mobile game like Candy Crush derives its revenue from a small fraction of users. For a traditional movie theater chain, Candy Crush is best categorized as:

options.A: A failed positioning strategy.
options.B: A failed attempt to exploit change.
options.C: An ill-advised "shaping industry structure" strategy.
options.D: An inability to overcome the threat of substitutes.

2yr-05.explanation: This is the "dark side" example from your teaching script and the HBR article. IBM did shape industry structure, but it did so badly. By opening its architecture, it "encouraged price-based rivalry" and "shifted power to suppliers." This move, designed to grow the market, ultimately destroyed the industry's profitability for all PC makers (including itself) by creating two monstrously powerful suppliers.
2yr-05.stem: In the 1980s, IBM standardized its PC components ("open architecture") to grow the market, which accidentally ceded all long-term profit to two suppliers, Microsoft and Intel. This is a "dark side" example of:

options.A: When their core technology is more than 10% different.
options.B: When they are sold to customers in different geographic regions.
options.C: When the underlying structure of the Five Forces is markedly different for each.
options.D: When one is a "product" and the other is a "service."

2yr-05.explanation: This is a key, and often missed, point from the article's "Defining the Relevant Industry" sidebar. The definition of an industry is not based on the product itself, but on its competitive structure. Automotive oil (sold to fragmented, price-sensitive consumers) and truck oil (sold to powerful, sophisticated fleet buyers) have completely different buyer power, supplier power, and rivalry structures. Therefore, they are different industries requiring different strategies.
2yr-05.stem: According to Porter, when are two products (e.g., automotive motor oil vs. heavy-truck motor oil) considered part of different industries, even if they appear similar?

options.A: Because high growth and technology are "factors," not "forces," and do not guarantee profitability.
options.B: Because high growth attracts a flood of new entrants, and rapid tech change can empower suppliers (like Nvidia).
options.C: Because high growth eliminates rivalry, which is necessary for a healthy industry.
options.D: Both (a) and (b).

2yr-05.explanation: This question directly targets the "Factors, not Forces" pitfall. (a) is the correct concept, and (b) provides the correct mechanism. Fast-growing, "sexy" industries (like the early PC industry or the current EV "shakeout") are often traps. High growth mutes rivalry but also acts as a beacon, attracting a flood of new entrants. Simultaneously, rapid tech change can create new, powerful suppliers (like Nvidia) who provide the critical "picks and shovels" and capture all the value.
2yr-05.stem: An industry is experiencing 50% annual growth and rapid technological innovation. According to Porter, why might this industry be profoundly unattractive?

options.A: The buyer has high bargaining leverage and high price sensitivity.
options.B: The buyer has high bargaining leverage but low price sensitivity.
options.C: The buyer has low bargaining leverage and low price sensitivity.
options.D: The buyer has low bargaining leverage but high price sensitivity.

2yr-05.explanation: This is a very nuanced distinction from the article. The buyer is powerful (high leverage) because they are large. However, they are not price-sensitive. Because the component is critical to their quality but a tiny fraction of their cost, they will not risk a lower-quality component to save a tiny amount of money. They will use their leverage to demand quality and reliability, not a lower price, which is less destructive to industry profits.
2yr-05.stem: A powerful B2B buyer (e.g., an automaker) purchases a component that represents only 1% of its total cost, but that component is absolutely critical to the performance and quality of its final product. How does this specifically affect the buyer's power?

options.A: It decreases the threat of new entrants, as they fear getting stuck.
options.B: It intensifies rivalry, especially during economic downturns.
options.C: It increases the bargaining power of suppliers, who know the firms cannot leave.
options.D: It decreases the bargaining power of buyers, who have fewer options.

2yr-05.explanation: This is a key driver of rivalry. High exit barriers mean that even when firms are earning low or negative returns, they cannot easily leave the market. This "stuck" capacity leads to desperate, profit-destroying behavior (i.e., price wars) as firms fight for the remaining market share, especially during downturns. This is a key driver of the "zero-sum" rivalry in your teaching script (e.g., the EV "shakeout").
2yr-05.stem: An industry has extremely high exit barriers (e.g., highly specialized, non-recoverable assets like a steel mill). What is the primary effect of this on the industry's structure?

options.A: Neutralize the bargaining power of suppliers.
options.B: Create a new substitute product.
options.C: Increase barriers to entry for other car makers.
options.D: Exploit a shift in government policy.

2yr-05.explanation: As your teaching script highlights, Nvidia is the "King of Suppliers" in the AI gold rush. Tesla recognizes that being dependent on a single, powerful supplier for its most critical future technology (AI) is a fatal strategic flaw. Building "Dojo" is a multi-billion-dollar "shaping" strategy to neutralize supplier power by vertically integrating, giving Tesla control over its own destiny.
2yr-05.stem: Tesla's decision to build its own "Dojo" AI supercomputer instead of just buying from Nvidia is a direct strategic attempt to:

options.A: Intense rivalry, as AmazonBasics competes with them.
options.B: Bargaining power of suppliers, as Amazon supplies the customers.
options.C: Bargaining power of buyers, as Amazon is the dominant, price-setting channel.
options.D: Threat of substitutes, as Amazon can replace them.

2yr-05.explanation: This is the "Amazon" case from your teaching script. In the "industry" of e-commerce sellers, Amazon is not the supplier; the sellers are. Amazon is the intermediate customer or channel. Because Amazon is highly concentrated (one platform) and the sellers are fragmented (1.9M), Amazon has immense buyer power to "force down prices" (via fees) and "demand better service" (via FBA), capturing all the profit.
2yr-05.stem: In the relationship between the 1.9 million 3rd-party sellers and the Amazon Marketplace platform, Amazon's power is best described as:

options.A: Because they are only relevant in high-tech industries.
options.B: Because their impact is best understood through how they affect the existing five forces.
options.C: Because they are a "factor" (like technology) and not a "force."
options.D: Both (b) and (c).

2yr-05.explanation: This is a fine-grained distinction. (c) is true, but (b) is the reason why. Porter argues "Complementors" are not a separate force, but a factor whose impact is already captured by the model. For example, a strong app ecosystem (a complement) raises barriers to entry for a new phone OS and reduces the threat of substitutes, thus making the industry more attractive.
2yr-05.stem: The HBR article argues that "Complementors" (e.g., apps for an iPhone) are not a sixth force. Why?

options.A: A successful "positioning" strategy.
options.B: A successful "exploitation" of change.
options.C: A "zero-sum" rivalry outcome.
options.D: A "dark side" of "shaping" industry structure.

2yr-05.explanation: This is the IBM lesson. The company "won" the short-term battle for market share but "lost" the long-term war for industry profitability. By "shaping" the industry in a way that ceded power to other forces (suppliers, in this case), it destroyed its own long-term profit potential. This is a common and fatal strategic error.
2yr-05.stem: A company's strategic action successfully increases its market share and harms its rivals, but in the long run, it also lowers entry barriers and increases supplier power for the entire industry. This situation is best described as:

options.A: High fixed costs and low marginal costs.
options.B: High demand-side benefits of scale (network effects).
options.C: High supplier power from unionized labor.
options.D: A high threat of powerful substitutes.

2yr-05.explanation: This is a deep structural similarity identified in the HBR article. Both industries have massive fixed costs (planes, paper mills) and low marginal costs (one more passenger, one more ream of paper). This creates intense pressure to "fill capacity," which inevitably leads to price-cutting to steal incremental customers, driving down profits for everyone.
2yr-05.stem: The airline industry and the paper manufacturing industry both suffer from intense, price-based rivalry. What underlying structural characteristic do they share?

options.A: The expected retaliation from incumbents.
options.B: The availability of substitutes.
options.C: The power of suppliers in their home market.
options.D: The number of complementors available.

2yr-05.explanation: This is a key insight from the article. An industry might look attractive with low barriers, but if the existing incumbents (like Starbucks, as per the article) have a history of "vigorous and protracted" retaliation, it will deter entry. The expectation of a brutal fight is itself a barrier.
2yr-05.stem: A new entrant's decision to enter an industry is not just based on the height of the existing barriers but also on:

options.A: A decrease in buyer power.
options.B: An increase in the threat of new entrants.
options.C: A downstream or indirect substitute.
options.D: A shift in the power of complementors.

2yr-05.explanation: This is one of the most difficult concepts in the article ("downstream or indirect substitution"). The apartments are not a direct substitute (you can't "use" an apartment to fertilize a lawn). They are a downstream substitute because they replace the buyer industry's product (the single-family home with a lawn). If there are no lawns, there is no lawn-care industry.
2yr-05.stem: For the home lawn-care industry, the societal trend of building high-density urban apartments instead of suburban single-family homes represents what?

options.A: Is too complex to be used by most managers.
options.B: Over-emphasizes industry structure and ignores the importance of firm-specific resources and capabilities as drivers of profit.
options.C: Fails to account for the role of government.
options.D: Under-emphasizes the threat of substitutes.

2yr-05.explanation: This is the most famous academic criticism of Porter. Porter's model (and the SCP paradigm it's built on) implies that industry is the primary determinant of profit ("the game you play"). The RBV argues that firm-specific assets (e.g., Toyota's production system, Tesla's battery tech, a "Core Competency") are the real drivers of profit, allowing superior firms to win even in "terrible" industries. MCQ Sec B: (Inter-Force Dynamics & Criticisms) This set focuses on second-order effects (how forces interact), the nuances of industry definition, and the academic critiques of the framework.
2yr-05.stem: A key criticism of the Five Forces model, often associated with the "Resource-Based View" (RBV) of the firm, is that the model:

options.A: It will shift rivalry from price-based to feature-based.
options.B: It will intensify rivalry and shift it to a price-based, "zero-sum" game.
options.C: It will decrease rivalry as firms band together to fight the substitute.
options.D: It will increase supplier power for movie studios.

2yr-05.explanation: This tests second-order effects. The substitute (streaming) puts a hard ceiling on what rental stores can charge. As customers leave, the industry pie shrinks, and growth becomes negative. This intensifies rivalry among the remaining players (e.g., Blockbuster) who are now fighting for scraps. This rivalry will gravitate to price in a desperate, zero-sum battle for the remaining customers.
2yr-05.stem: The emergence of a powerful, low-cost substitute (e.g., digital streaming for video rentals) will most likely have what immediate effect on the nature of rivalry within the original video rental industry?

options.A: It will increase supplier power for hardware makers.
options.B: It will decrease buyer power as customers have more choice.
options.C: It will intensify rivalry by dramatically increasing the number of new entrants.
options.D: It will decrease the threat of substitutes.

2yr-05.explanation: This is another second-order effect. The primary effect is lowering the Threat of New Entrants. The immediate knock-on effect of that is a massive increase in the number of new entrants, which directly and intensely increases rivalry. The software industry is now flooded with new competitors because the cloud (a complement) removed the massive capital barrier of needing to build one's own data centers.
2yr-05.stem: A reduction in capital-requirement entry barriers (e.g., the rise of AWS/cloud computing for the software industry) will most likely have what immediate knock-on effect?

options.A: All banks use the same "SWIFT" technology standard.
options.B: The industry's profit pool is expanding in emerging markets.
options.C: Buyer power, supplier power, and regulatory barriers are radically different across countries.
options.D: All banks are equally vulnerable to the substitute of cryptocurrency.

2yr-05.explanation: This tests the "Defining the Relevant Industry" concept. An industry is only "global" if its structure is global. Retail banking is a classic multi-domestic industry. The power of buyers, the nature of regulation (a barrier), and the competitive landscape are not the same in India as they are in the United States. Therefore, a "global" strategy would fail; a firm needs a separate strategy for each distinct industry (country).
2yr-05.stem: Porter's analysis suggests that "global banking" is the incorrect industry definition to use for strategy-making if:

options.A: Focusing too much on "dividing the pie" (competition) and ignoring "growing the pie" (co-opetition).
options.B: Being too complex for modern managers.
options.C: Ignoring the power of government and technology.
options.D: Underestimating the "zero-sum" nature of all business.

2yr-05.explanation: This is the core of the "Game Theory" critique mentioned in the HBR article's footnotes. Porter's model is fundamentally about competition—how the pie of value is divided. The Complementors argument states that business is also about cooperation (or "co-opetition"). Firms like Intel and Microsoft cooperate to create and grow the pie (the PC market), which the Five Forces model doesn't fully capture.
2yr-05.stem: The "6th Force" (Complementors) argument, often associated with Adam Brandenburger and Barry Nalebuff, critiques Porter's model primarily for:

options.A: Because it is a form of corporate social responsibility that improves brand image.
options.B: Because the leader, by virtue of its size, will capture the largest share of the benefits from a better industry structure.
options.C: Because it allows the leader to create a "zero-sum" game.
options.D: Because it is a form of "expected retaliation" that deters new entrants.

2yr-05.explanation: This is a key insight on "shaping" strategy from the article. If an industry's structure is "bad" (e.g., fragmented, low-tech), it's a "public good" to fix it. The leader (Sysco) is the only one with the resources to do so (e.g., invest in IT, create private labels). While this helps all firms, the leader, with its dominant market share, will disproportionately benefit, making it a high-ROI strategic investment.
2yr-05.stem: The HBR article states that an industry leader (like Sysco) should invest in improving industry structure, even if it's a "public good" that helps rivals. Why is this often the leader's most profitable strategic opportunity?

options.A: Increases the "Bargaining Power of Suppliers" by giving labor the ability to capture value through higher wages.
options.B: Increases "Rivalry" as firms must compete for the best workers.
options.C: Decreases "Barriers to Entry" as new firms can hire the same workers.
options.D: Increases "Threat of Substitutes" as firms will seek to automate.

2yr-05.explanation: This tests the definition of a supplier. A "supplier" is any input provider. As the article states, "powerful suppliers, including suppliers of labor," can squeeze profitability. A strong union acts as a concentrated supplier, giving it immense Bargaining Power of Suppliers to negotiate for (capture) a large portion of the industry's value in the form of wages and benefits, thus depressing industry profits.
2yr-05.stem: An industry's primary "suppliers" are a highly skilled, specialized, and heavily unionized workforce. This structural feature primarily:

options.A: An increase in supplier power.
options.B: A shift from zero-sum to positive-sum rivalry.
options.C: Intense, destructive, price-based rivalry.
options.D: A rapid increase in the threat of substitutes.

2yr-05.explanation: This combines two key drivers of Rivalry from the HBR article. Slowing growth means firms must steal share from each other to grow. High exit barriers mean no one can leave the "game." The result is a "perfect storm": a large number of "stuck" competitors fighting for a shrinking pie, which inevitably leads to destructive, margin-eroding price wars.
2yr-05.stem: An industry is experiencing both slowing growth (after an initial boom) and high exit barriers (massive, specialized factories). This combination is a "perfect storm" for:

options.A: Because it is only relevant as a barrier to entry.
options.B: Because its impact on profitability is ambiguous and is determined by how it affects the five forces.
options.C: Because it is a "macro" factor, unlike the "micro" forces.
options.D: Because it is a "complementor," which is a separate force.

2yr-05.explanation: This is the core of the "Factors vs. Forces" argument. Technology is not inherently good or bad for profitability. Its impact is ambiguous. The internet destroyed profitability in some industries (e.g., travel agents, by lowering barriers and increasing buyer power) while increasing it in others (e.g., creating platform network effects). You must analyze technology through the lens of the five forces.
2yr-05.stem: Why is "Technology" not a force?

options.A: They are fragmented, face high switching costs, and the product is highly differentiated.
options.B: They are concentrated, face low switching costs, and the product is standardized.
options.C: The industry they are buying from is growing rapidly.
options.D: The product they are buying is a "complement" to their main business.

2yr-05.explanation: This is the "nightmare" scenario for a seller, combining all the key drivers of buyer power from the article. Concentrated buyers (e.g., 3-4 powerful automakers) buying from standardized suppliers (e.g., commodity seat-belts) with low switching costs (they can swap suppliers easily) means the buyers have all the leverage to force prices down to the bare minimum.
2yr-05.stem: A buyer group's power is highest when:

options.A: The bargaining power of suppliers.
options.B: The bargaining power of intermediate buyers (i.e., dealership channels).
options.C: The threat of substitutes.
options.D: The threat of new entrants.

2yr-05.explanation: This tests the "intermediate customers" concept. In the traditional auto industry, the dealerships are a powerful intermediate buyer channel. They control customer access and capture a significant margin. By "shaping" the industry with a D2C model, a company neutralizes this powerful buyer force, allowing it to control the customer experience and retain 100% of the profit margin.
2yr-05.stem: A company's strategic shift to a Direct-to-Consumer (D2C) model (like Tesla's) is a direct attempt to neutralize which force?

options.A: Incumbents will invest heavily in advertising and R&D to differentiate.
options.B: A "shakeout" will occur where weaker firms are acquired or go bankrupt.
options.C: Industry-wide profitability will be stable and consistently high.
options.D: Firms will attempt to create "positive-sum" competition by finding niches.

2yr-05.explanation: This is a tricky "least likely" question. High barriers to entry (which is "good") do not guarantee high profits if Rivalry is intense (which is "bad"). The U.S. auto industry is a perfect example: barriers are high, but rivalry is so intense that profits are low. Therefore, "stable and consistently high" profits are the least likely outcome. (a), (b), and (d) are all common outcomes of this structure.
2yr-05.stem: Which of the following is the least likely outcome of an industry structure with both high barriers to entry and intense, price-based rivalry?

options.A: New Entrant; Rival
options.B: Substitute; New Entrant
options.C: Rival; Substitute
options.D: Supplier; Buyer

2yr-05.explanation: This case from the teaching script tests the evolution of a threat. Initially, Rapido was not a rival to Uber/Ola's 4-wheel business; it was a substitute, performing the "job" of urban transport by a different means (2-wheel). Once it had 50 million users, it used that strength to "jump" industries and become a new entrant into the 4-wheel cab industry, where it is now a direct rival.
2yr-05.stem: When Rapido entered the Indian ride-hailing market with 2-wheel bike-taxis, it initially represented a(n) ________. When it used its user base to launch its own 4-wheel cab service, it became a(n) ________.

options.A: A major economic recession.
options.B: The rise of the internet.
options.C: A new, powerful government regulation.
options.D: A trend toward vertical integration.

2yr-05.explanation: This tests the systemic impact of a major factor. The internet (a "technology factor") is famous for its "dark side" effects on industry structure, as noted in Porter's 2001 HBR article "Strategy and the Internet": It lowered entry barriers (e.g., e-commerce vs. brick-and-mortar). It increased buyer power (e.g., price comparison websites). It increased the threat of substitutes (e.g., streaming vs. CDs, Zoom vs. travel).
2yr-05.stem: Which of the following "factors" has the potential to simultaneously lower barriers to entry, increase buyer power, and increase the threat of substitutes?

options.A: Reduce the firm's per-unit cost as production increases.
options.B: Limit the willingness of customers to buy from a newcomer, reducing the price the entrant can command.
options.C: Allow the firm to get better terms from its suppliers.
options.D: Guarantee government support as a "utility."

2yr-05.explanation: This question forces a distinction between the two types of scale economies from the article. (a) is supply-side economies of scale (getting cheaper with size). Demand-side benefits (network effects, like Facebook's) mean the value of the product increases with the number of users. This is a barrier because a new entrant with zero users (a new social network) offers zero value to a new customer, making it incredibly difficult to get the first 1,000, let alone 1 million, users.
2yr-05.stem: A firm's "demand-side benefits of scale" (network effects) are a powerful barrier to entry because they:

options.A: A firm's conduct (strategy) determines its performance, which in turn shapes the industry structure.
options.B: The structure of an industry (the Five Forces) determines the conduct (strategies) of firms, which in turn determines their performance (profitability).
options.C: A firm's performance (profits) determines its conduct (strategy) and the industry's structure.
options.D: These three elements are unrelated and should be analyzed separately.

2yr-05.explanation: This is the deep, academic theory underlying the entire framework. The SCP paradigm is a one-way street: The industry's Structure (the "game," i.e., the Five Forces) is the independent variable. This structure dictates the range of possible strategic Conduct (the "moves," i.e., positioning, shaping). That conduct, in turn, leads to Performance (the "outcome," i.e., profits). This is why Porter's first step is always to analyze the industry structure.
2yr-05.stem: Porter's framework is rooted in the "Structure-Conduct-Performance" (SCP) paradigm of industrial organization economics. What is the central argument of this paradigm?

options.A: Rivalry has not yet become intense enough to drive consolidation.
options.B: The high growth rate itself is a "factor" that has attracted a flood of new entrants, and powerful, concentrated suppliers (like AI platform providers) are capturing all the value.
options.C: The threat of substitutes is unexpectedly high, as traditional R&D methods are still more effective.
options.D: Buyer power is low because the technology is complex, which should lead to high profitability.

2yr-05.explanation: This question directly targets the "Factors, not Forces" pitfall. High growth is a "factor," not a guarantee of profit. As the HBR article warns, "a narrow focus on growth is one of the major causes of bad strategy decisions." High growth often (1) attracts a flood of new entrants, which intensifies rivalry, and (2) can create immensely powerful suppliers (like Nvidia, as per the teaching script) who provide the critical "picks and shovels" and capture all the value, leaving none for the firms competing in the "sexy" industry itself.
2yr-05.stem: A new entrant in a high-growth, "sexy" industry (e.g., AI-driven drug discovery) attracts massive venture capital funding. However, the industry's profitability remains near zero. According to Porter, what is the most likely structural explanation?

options.A: Shaping industry structure by expanding the profit pool.
options.B: Positioning the company where the competitive forces are weakest.
options.C: Exploiting industry change by creating a new substitute.
options.D: Neutralizing supplier power through vertical integration.

2yr-05.explanation: This is the exact Paccar strategy from the HBR article and teaching script. The company is not trying to change the "terrible" structure of the entire airline industry. Instead, it is engaging in Positioning. It has identified a "foxhole" or niche segment (owner-operators in Paccar's case, executives here) where the force of Buyer Power is weak, allowing it to escape the intense, price-based rivalry of the main industry.
2yr-05.stem: A company in a structurally "terrible" industry (e.g., airlines) invests heavily to exclusively serve a small, fragmented customer niche (e.g., high-net-worth executives) that is far less price-sensitive and demands hyper-customized service. According to Porter, this is a classic example of:

options.A: A failed positioning strategy.
options.B: A failed attempt to exploit change.
options.C: An ill-advised "shaping industry structure" strategy.
options.D: An inability to overcome the threat of substitutes.

2yr-05.explanation: This is the "dark side" example from the teaching script and HBR article. IBM did shape industry structure, but it did so badly. By opening its architecture, it "encouraged price-based rivalry" and "shifted power to suppliers." This move, designed to grow the market, ultimately destroyed the industry's profitability for all PC makers (including itself) by creating two monstrously powerful suppliers.
2yr-05.stem: In the 1980s, IBM standardized its PC components ("open architecture") to grow the market, which accidentally ceded all long-term profit to two suppliers, Microsoft and Intel. This is a "dark side" example of:

options.A: A new entrant.
options.B: A substitute.
options.C: A rival.
options.D: A complementor.

2yr-05.explanation: This tests the "job-to-be-done" concept from the teaching script (e.g., Twitter vs. TikTok). The "job" a movie theater sells is "leisure time" or "filling 90 minutes of downtime." A mobile game performs the exact same job through a different means. It is not a rival (it's not a theater) or a new entrant (it's not entering the theater industry). It is a powerful substitute that competes for the customer's time and leisure budget.
2yr-05.stem: A free-to-play mobile game like Candy Crush derives its revenue from a small fraction of users. For a traditional movie theater chain, Candy Crush is best categorized as:

options.A: When their core technology is more than 10% different.
options.B: When they are sold to customers in different geographic regions.
options.C: When the underlying structure of the Five Forces is markedly different for each.
options.D: When one is a "product" and the other is a "service."

2yr-05.explanation: This is a key, and often missed, point from the article's "Defining the Relevant Industry" sidebar. The definition of an industry is not based on the product itself, but on its competitive structure. Automotive oil (sold to fragmented, price-sensitive consumers) and truck oil (sold to powerful, sophisticated fleet buyers) have completely different buyer power, supplier power, and rivalry structures. Therefore, they are different industries requiring different strategies.
2yr-05.stem: According to Porter, when are two products (e.g., automotive motor oil vs. heavy-truck motor oil) considered part of different industries, even if they appear similar?

options.A: The buyer has high bargaining leverage and high price sensitivity.
options.B: The buyer has high bargaining leverage but low price sensitivity.
options.C: The buyer has low bargaining leverage and low price sensitivity.
options.D: The buyer has low bargaining leverage but high price sensitivity.

2yr-05.explanation: This is a very nuanced distinction from the article. The buyer is powerful (high leverage) because they are large. However, they are not price-sensitive. Because the component is critical to their quality but a tiny fraction of their cost, they will not risk a lower-quality component to save a tiny amount of money. They will use their leverage to demand quality and reliability, not a lower price, which is less destructive to industry profits.
2yr-05.stem: A powerful B2B buyer (e.g., an automaker) purchases a component that represents only 1% of its total cost, but that component is absolutely critical to the performance and quality of its final product. How does this specifically affect the buyer's power?

options.A: It decreases the threat of new entrants, as they fear getting stuck.
options.B: It intensifies rivalry, especially during economic downturns.
options.C: It increases the bargaining power of suppliers, who know the firms cannot leave.
options.D: It decreases the bargaining power of buyers, who have fewer options.

2yr-05.explanation: This is a key driver of rivalry. High exit barriers mean that even when firms are earning low or negative returns, they cannot easily leave the market. This "stuck" capacity leads to desperate, profit-destroying behavior (i.e., price wars) as firms fight for the remaining market share, especially during downturns. This is a key driver of the "zero-sum" rivalry in the teaching script (e.g., the EV "shakeout").
2yr-05.stem: An industry has extremely high exit barriers (e.g., highly specialized, non-recoverable assets like a steel mill). What is the primary effect of this on the industry's structure?

options.A: Neutralize the bargaining power of suppliers.
options.B: Create a new substitute product.
options.C: Increase barriers to entry for other car makers.
options.D: Exploit a shift in government policy.

2yr-05.explanation: As the teaching script highlights, Nvidia is the "King of Suppliers" in the AI gold rush. Tesla recognizes that being dependent on a single, powerful supplier for its most critical future technology (AI) is a fatal strategic flaw. Building "Dojo" is a multi-billion-dollar "shaping" strategy to neutralize supplier power by vertically integrating, giving Tesla control over its own destiny.
2yr-05.stem: Tesla's decision to build its own "Dojo" AI supercomputer instead of just buying from Nvidia is a direct strategic attempt to:

options.A: Intense rivalry, as AmazonBasics competes with them.
options.B: Bargaining power of suppliers, as Amazon supplies the customers.
options.C: Bargaining power of buyers, as Amazon is the dominant, price-setting channel.
options.D: Threat of substitutes, as Amazon can replace them.

2yr-05.explanation: This is the "Amazon" case from the teaching script. In the "industry" of e-commerce sellers, Amazon is not the supplier; the sellers are. Amazon is the intermediate customer or channel. Because Amazon is highly concentrated (one platform) and the sellers are fragmented (1.9M), Amazon has immense buyer power to "force down prices" (via fees) and "demand better service" (via FBA), capturing all the profit.
2yr-05.stem: In the relationship between the 1.9 million 3rd-party sellers and the Amazon Marketplace platform, Amazon's power is best described as:

options.A: Because they are only relevant in high-tech industries.
options.B: Because their impact is best understood through how they affect the existing five forces.
options.C: Because they are a "factor" (like technology) and not a "force."
options.D: Both (b) and (c).

2yr-05.explanation: This is a fine-grained distinction. (c) is true, but (b) is the reason why. Porter argues "Complementors" are not a separate force, but a factor whose impact is already captured by the model. For example, a strong app ecosystem (a complement) raises barriers to entry for a new phone OS and reduces the threat of substitutes, thus making the industry more attractive.
2yr-05.stem: The HBR article argues that "Complementors" (e.g., apps for an iPhone) are not a sixth force. Why?

options.A: A successful "positioning" strategy.
options.B: A successful "exploitation" of change.
options.C: A "zero-sum" rivalry outcome.
options.D: A "dark side" of "shaping" industry structure.

2yr-05.explanation: This is the IBM lesson. The company "won" the short-term battle for market share but "lost" the long-term war for industry profitability. By "shaping" the industry in a way that ceded power to other forces (suppliers, in this case), it destroyed its own long-term profit potential. This is a common and fatal strategic error.
2yr-05.stem: A company's strategic action successfully increases its market share and harms its rivals, but in the long run, it also lowers entry barriers and increases supplier power for the entire industry. This situation is best described as:

options.A: High fixed costs and low marginal costs.
options.B: High demand-side benefits of scale (network effects).
options.C: High supplier power from unionized labor.
options.D: A high threat of powerful substitutes.

2yr-05.explanation: This is a deep structural similarity identified in the HBR article. Both industries have massive fixed costs (planes, paper mills) and low marginal costs (one more passenger, one more ream of paper). This creates intense pressure to "fill capacity," which inevitably leads to price-cutting to steal incremental customers, driving down profits for everyone.
2yr-05.stem: The airline industry and the paper manufacturing industry both suffer from intense, price-based rivalry. What underlying structural characteristic do they share?

options.A: The expected retaliation from incumbents.
options.B: The availability of substitutes.
options.C: The power of suppliers in their home market.
options.D: The number of complementors available.

2yr-05.explanation: This is a key insight from the article. An industry might look attractive with low barriers, but if the existing incumbents (like Starbucks, as per the article) have a history of "vigorous and protracted" retaliation, it will deter entry. The expectation of a brutal fight is itself a barrier.
2yr-05.stem: A new entrant's decision to enter an industry is not just based on the height of the existing barriers but also on:

options.A: A decrease in buyer power.
options.B: An increase in the threat of new entrants.
options.C: A downstream or indirect substitute.
options.D: A shift in the power of complementors.

2yr-05.explanation: This is one of the most difficult concepts in the article ("downstream or indirect substitution"). The apartments are not a direct substitute (you can't "use" an apartment to fertilize a lawn). They are a downstream substitute because they replace the buyer industry's product (the single-family home with a lawn). If there are no lawns, there is no lawn-care industry.
2yr-05.stem: For the home lawn-care industry, the societal trend of building high-density urban apartments instead of suburban single-family homes represents what?

options.A: Is too complex to be used by most managers.
options.B: Over-emphasizes industry structure and ignores the importance of firm-specific resources and capabilities as drivers of profit.
options.C: Fails to account for the role of government.
options.D: Under-emphasizes the threat of substitutes.

2yr-05.explanation: This is the most famous academic criticism of Porter. Porter's model (and the SCP paradigm it's built on) implies that industry is the primary determinant of profit ("the game you play"). The RBV argues that firm-specific assets (e.g., Toyota's production system, Tesla's battery tech, a "Core Competency") are the real drivers of profit, allowing superior firms to win even in "terrible" industries. MCQ Set 2: Advanced Concepts (Inter-Force Dynamics & Criticisms) This set focuses on second-order effects (how forces interact), the nuances of industry definition, and the academic critiques of the framework.
2yr-05.stem: A key criticism of the Five Forces model, often associated with the "Resource-Based View" (RBV) of the firm, is that the model:

options.A: It will shift rivalry from price-based to feature-based.
options.B: It will intensify rivalry and shift it to a price-based, "zero-sum" game.
options.C: It will decrease rivalry as firms band together to fight the substitute.
options.D: It will increase supplier power for movie studios.

2yr-05.explanation: This tests second-order effects. The substitute (streaming) puts a hard ceiling on what rental stores can charge. As customers leave, the industry pie shrinks, and growth becomes negative. This intensifies rivalry among the remaining players (e.g., Blockbuster) who are now fighting for scraps. This rivalry will gravitate to price in a desperate, zero-sum battle for the remaining customers.
2yr-05.stem: The emergence of a powerful, low-cost substitute (e.g., digital streaming for video rentals) will most likely have what immediate effect on the nature of rivalry within the original video rental industry?

options.A: It will increase supplier power for hardware makers.
options.B: It will decrease buyer power as customers have more choice.
options.C: It will intensify rivalry by dramatically increasing the number of new entrants.
options.D: It will decrease the threat of substitutes.

2yr-05.explanation: This is another second-order effect. The primary effect is lowering the Threat of New Entrants. The immediate knock-on effect of that is a massive increase in the number of new entrants, which directly and intensely increases rivalry. The software industry is now flooded with new competitors because the cloud (a complement) removed the massive capital barrier of needing to build one's own data centers.
2yr-05.stem: A reduction in capital-requirement entry barriers (e.g., the rise of AWS/cloud computing for the software industry) will most likely have what immediate knock-on effect?

options.A: All banks use the same "SWIFT" technology standard.
options.B: The industry's profit pool is expanding in emerging markets.
options.C: Buyer power, supplier power, and regulatory barriers are radically different across countries.
options.D: All banks are equally vulnerable to the substitute of cryptocurrency.

2yr-05.explanation: This tests the "Defining the Relevant Industry" concept. An industry is only "global" if its structure is global. Retail banking is a classic multi-domestic industry. The power of buyers, the nature of regulation (a barrier), and the competitive landscape are not the same in India as they are in the United States. Therefore, a "global" strategy would fail; a firm needs a separate strategy for each distinct industry (country).
2yr-05.stem: Porter's analysis suggests that "global banking" is the incorrect industry definition to use for strategy-making if:

options.A: Focusing too much on "dividing the pie" (competition) and ignoring "growing the pie" (co-opetition).
options.B: Being too complex for modern managers.
options.C: Ignoring the power of government and technology.
options.D: Underestimating the "zero-sum" nature of all business.

2yr-05.explanation: This is the core of the "Game Theory" critique mentioned in the HBR article's footnotes. Porter's model is fundamentally about competition—how the pie of value is divided. The Complementors argument states that business is also about cooperation (or "co-opetition"). Firms like Intel and Microsoft cooperate to create and grow the pie (the PC market), which the Five Forces model doesn't fully capture.
2yr-05.stem: The "6th Force" (Complementors) argument, often associated with Adam Brandenburger and Barry Nalebuff, critiques Porter's model primarily for:

options.A: Because it is a form of corporate social responsibility that improves brand image.
options.B: Because the leader, by virtue of its size, will capture the largest share of the benefits from a better industry structure.
options.C: Because it allows the leader to create a "zero-sum" game.
options.D: Because it is a form of "expected retaliation" that deters new entrants.

2yr-05.explanation: This is a key insight on "shaping" strategy from the article. If an industry's structure is "bad" (e.g., fragmented, low-tech), it's a "public good" to fix it. The leader (Sysco) is the only one with the resources to do so (e.g., invest in IT, create private labels). While this helps all firms, the leader, with its dominant market share, will disproportionately benefit, making it a high-ROI strategic investment.
2yr-05.stem: The HBR article states that an industry leader (like Sysco) should invest in improving industry structure, even if it's a "public good" that helps rivals. Why is this often the leader's most profitable strategic opportunity?

options.A: Increases the "Bargaining Power of Suppliers" by giving labor the ability to capture value through higher wages.
options.B: Increases "Rivalry" as firms must compete for the best workers.
options.C: Decreases "Barriers to Entry" as new firms can hire the same workers.
options.D: Increases "Threat of Substitutes" as firms will seek to automate.

2yr-05.explanation: This tests the definition of a supplier. A "supplier" is any input provider. As the article states, "powerful suppliers, including suppliers of labor," can squeeze profitability. A strong union acts as a concentrated supplier, giving it immense Bargaining Power of Suppliers to negotiate for (capture) a large portion of the industry's value in the form of wages and benefits, thus depressing industry profits.

options.A: An increase in supplier power.
options.B: A shift from zero-sum to positive-sum rivalry.
options.C: Intense, destructive, price-based rivalry.
options.D: A rapid increase in the threat of substitutes.

options.B: Because its impact on profitability is ambiguous and is determined by how it affects the five forces.
options.C: Because it is a "macro" factor, unlike the "micro" forces.
options.D: Because it is a "complementor," which is a separate force.
